2. Request for Information 
CMS is soliciting public comment on how prior authorization for laboratory tests and DMEPOS 
items impacts patient care and health care provider burden, and if there are opportunities to 
mitigate burden. CMS is interested in how automation of the prior authorization process for 
DMEPOS items and laboratory services could benefit health care providers, payers, and 
patients, as well as other opportunities for improving these processes. 
â— How do prior authorization requirements for laboratory tests and DMEPOS items 
currently impact patient care and health care provider burden? 
Prior authorization (PA) requirements in place by most health insurance plans are designed such 
that the ordering provider would submit the PA request, wait for the response from the payor, 
and then bring the patient back to clinic for a blood draw or buccal swab to initiate testing. This 
process creates incredible burden on the ordering provider, as they must add this process to 
their clinicâ€™s workflow, determine appropriate CPT codes from the laboratory (not having the 
awareness that different payors have requested laboratories to bill the same test using different 
coding schemes), and then have the patient return for sample collection. Many patients live far 
away from ordering provider, so returning for sample collection is burdensome for the patient 
and their care team. This may result in the test never being performed. For those tests that are 
ultimately ordered, test initiation is delayed, which delays answers for families as well as any 
benefits the patient receives from a diagnosis.  
These PA requirements can be especially detrimental for genomic testing, as germline testing 
can be performed on a blood or buccal sample that can be readily collected on the same day 
that the provider decided to order the test and be held until authorization is received. 
Additionally, laboratories have worked directly with payors to understand each payorâ€™s billing 
and coding requirements, and they can submit prior authorization requests on behalf of the 
ordering provider and patient (using the clinical documentation supplied by the ordering 
provider to support medical necessity) as soon as a sample is received and communicate any 
follow up to the patient regarding denied prior authorizations and expected out of pocket costs. 
However, many payors will not allow the laboratory to initiate the prior authorization and/or 
require that the prior authorization be initiated prior to the date of service, which they define as 
the day that the sample was collected. Sample collection date is an arbitrary date of service for 
genomic testing and requiring that prior authorization requests be initiated prior to that date is 
a burden on patients that ultimately restricts access to care. Lastly, delayed reviews of prior 
authorization requests again delays initiation of testing, diagnosis, and treatments associated 
with diagnoses.

â— What are possible outcomes of more MACs, MA plans, or non-Medicare payers 
allowing a TRF to be valid medical documentation to show that a laboratory test is reasonable 
and necessary? 
When completed by an ordering provider, the TRF contains valuable information related to the 
indication for testing. TRFs can be created to highlight relevant portions of the medical history 
that support medical necessity and reduce the administrative burden of providing medical 
records. Such TRFs should be allowable without additional medical records, provided that 
sufficient detail is present. Appropriate safeguards must be in place, however, to ensure that 
this information is provided by the ordering provider and is supported by clinical records, when 
requested. Bad actors in the laboratory space have attempted to use the TRF without clinical 
records to support the payment of fraudulent claims, and the oversight required to monitor for 
fraudulent laboratories creates additional hurdles for established laboratories. 
 
â— How frequently are prior authorizations denied because the request was submitted 
after the specimen was collected? 
Our internal data shows that a relatively significant number of prior authorizations are denied 
due to requests being submitted after the collection date. To expound upon a previous 
comment, rare disease patients and their families face disproportionate access barriers to care, 
including long travel distances to specialty clinics, limited appointment availability, caregiving 
complexity, and reliance on special transportation or time away from work. For many families, 
requiring a second visit solely to collect a sample after prior authorization is obtained is difficult 
and, in practice, often unrealistic. Ordering clinicians are acutely aware that loss to follow-up is 
high when testing requires an additional visit and that delays or missed testing can materially 
affect diagnostic outcomes. As a result, clinicians reasonably prefer to collect the sample at the 
time the clinical decision to test is made, while the patient is present, even when prior 
authorization is still pending. Importantly, this approach does not expose the ordering provider 
to financial or compliance risk: if prior authorization is denied, the laboratoryâ€”not the 
physicianâ€”bears the risk of non-payment and testing can be cancelled prior to initiation. 
Treating specimen collection as an irreversible â€œdate of serviceâ€ misaligns utilization 
management policy with clinical reality and disproportionately restricts access for patients with 
rare and complex conditions.

â— What impacts have laboratory benefit managers (LBMs) had in facilitating prior 
authorization processes, regulating access, and controlling payment for laboratory services? 
LBMs have impacted all of these elements in some positive ways, including consolidating 
multiple payors under one umbrella related to PA submission process and medical necessity 
criteria. Elements of coverage and billing are less piecemeal and, broadly speaking, consistent. 
Additionally, they provide specialty expertise and support for smaller and/or regional health 
plans that may not be able to employ such staff. However, there are additional layers of 
complexity created by LBMs. Not all payers utilize all services offered by the LBM; in other 
words, they instead customize their agreement. Payors can choose which coverage guidelines 
and reimbursement policies to adopt, may utilize the LBM for appeal management or may keep 
in house, and may have claim edits in their system that do not align with LBM criteria used for 
prior authorization reviews. Laboratories as well as ordering providers do not have full insights 
into those deviations. Applicable coverage guidelines, billing requirements, and appeal follow 
up are unclear and can result in prior authorization and/or claim denials due to processes not 
be followed as expected by the payor.  Communication regarding issues and pathways for 
questions often become feedback loops, with the LBM stating that the laboratory needs to talk 
to the payor while the payor directs the laboratory to the LBM. The inability to discuss issues 
with either the payor or the LBM creates delays in access to care and, ultimately, harm to 
patients. Additionally, because LBMs are creating policy for a large population, outlier cases may 
fall into gaps with limited opportunities for coverage. 
â— What opportunities for process improvement exist for prior authorization 
requirements? Are changes needed to make requirements even more effective at containing 
costs, reducing burden, and improving patient outcomes? 
It may be helpful to acknowledge that date-of-service concepts are especially problematic in the 
laboratory context because workflows and specimen requirements vary. Not all laboratories are 
able to hold specimens indefinitely while awaiting prior authorization, and some specimen 
types require stabilization or preparatory steps (e.g., DNA extraction) upon receipt to preserve 
sample integrity, resulting in limited upfront cost even though analytical testing has not begun 
and can still be cancelled if authorization is denied. Further, at least one payer has publicly 
recommended that physicians retain specimens in their offices until prior authorization is 
obtained before sending them to the laboratory; however, most physician practices are not 
equipped to store, track, or manage biological specimens, even those stable at room 
temperature, and are understandably unwilling to assume this operational and liability burden. 
These dynamics underscore why reliance on specimen collection date as a proxy for service

GeneDx.com  
 
delivery is poorly suited to laboratory services and can unintentionally increase administrative 
burden, delay care, and exacerbate loss to follow up without improving utilization management 
or program integrity. 
In the laboratory context, prior authorization compliance and financial risk rest with the 
performing laboratory, not the ordering provider. When a specimen is submitted to a laboratory, 
the laboratory assumes responsibility for confirming coverage requirements, submitting prior 
authorization requests where applicable, and determining whether testing should proceed. If 
prior authorization is denied, laboratories can and do cancel testing prior to initiation and bear 
the associated risk of non-payment. Ordering providers do not bill for laboratory testing and are 
not financially exposed when authorization is not obtained. Policies that treat specimen 
collection by the clinician as service delivery, and limit prior authorization submission to the 
ordering provider, misallocate accountability and undermine established workflows in which 
laboratories function as the risk-bearing, accountable entity for utilization management. 
The limitations of date-of-service concepts are especially evident in urgent testing scenarios, 
such as NICU and prenatal genomic testing, where rapid diagnosis is clinically critical. In these 
cases, prior authorization may be waived or requested on an emergency basis, reflecting 
recognition that delays associated with standard prior authorization workflows are incompatible 
with patient care needs. These scenarios demonstrate that utilization management is most 
effectively aligned to whether testing proceedsâ€”not the specific calendar date associated with 
specimen collection. Importantly, laboratories continue to bear financial risk in these urgent 
contexts, reinforcing that payment risk, rather than rigid date requirements, is the primary 
safeguard against inappropriate utilization. 
â— How could automation of the prior authorization process for laboratory tests and 
DMEPOS items positively affect patient outcomes and potentially reduce both payer and health 
care provider burden? 
Automation of the prior authorization process for laboratory tests and DMEPOS items has 
significant potential to improve patient outcomes while reducing administrative burden for 
providers and payers, as demonstrated in the pharmacy benefit space where real-time 
electronic prior authorization enables timely access to therapy when standardized clinical 
criteria are met. For laboratory services, similar principles can be applied by automating intake, 
documentation validation, and payer communication to meaningfully shorten authorization 
turnaround times, reduce incomplete or duplicative submissions, and improve consistency in 
medical necessity review through structured clinical data capture. When designed 
appropriately, automated workflows can enable laboratoriesâ€”acting on behalf of ordering 
 
GeneDx, LLC  
205 & 207 Perry Parkway, Gaithersburg, MD 20877  
888-729-1206 | support@genedx.com  
GeneDx.com  
 
providersâ€”to initiate prior authorization requests, validate completeness of documentation, 
flag missing information in real time, and support faster payer review without delaying patient 
care. Advances in artificial intelligence can further strengthen these processes by rapidly 
analyzing accompanying medical records against payer criteria, identifying inconsistencies or 
omissions prior to submission, and detecting potential fraud, waste, or abuse through analysis 
of ordering patterns and utilization trends at scale. Importantly, automation should focus on 
streamlining administrative and documentation-driven components of prior authorization 
rather than relying solely on diagnosis or procedure codes, which are often insufficiently specific 
for complex services such as rare disease genomic testing. By shifting routine, administrative 
elements into automated and AI-enabled systems, payers can preserve robust program integrity 
while providers and laboratories achieve more timely access to medically necessary testing 
without increasing utilization risk.  
 
Experience in the pharmacy benefit space demonstrates that automation of prior authorization 
can materially improve access to care while preserving appropriate utilization management. 
Real-time electronic prior authorization for many medications has been enabled by 
standardized data exchange, transparent payer criteria, and automated validation of clinical 
requirements, allowing routine requests to be approved quickly while reserving manual review 
for exceptions. Similar principles can be applied to laboratory services by automating intake, 
documentation completeness checks, and payer communication, thereby reducing turnaround 
times and administrative burden for clinicians, laboratories, and payers alike. 
 
â— What other issues exist regarding prior authorization processes for laboratory tests and 
DMEPOS items that technology is not currently addressing? What opportunities exist for 
technology to mitigate those issues? 
While automation and technology have improved prior authorization workflows in certain 
areas, several persistent issues remain unaddressed for laboratory tests and DMEPOS itemsâ€”
particularly for complex and specialized services such as genomic testing. A primary gap is the 
lack of alignment between prior authorization systems, claims processing logic, and clinical 
workflows, which can result in denials or delays unrelated to medical necessity despite 
complete and appropriate submissions. Technology has also not adequately addressed 
inconsistencies across payers and laboratory benefit managers (LBMs) regarding documentation 
 
GeneDx, LLC  
205 & 207 Perry Parkway, Gaithersburg, MD 20877  
888-729-1206 | support@genedx.com  
GeneDx.com  
 
requirements, coverage criteria, procedure coding, and submission pathways, creating 
confusion and inefficiency for providers and laboratories alike. 
 
Additional challenges include limited visibility into authorization status across systems, 
constrained mechanisms for real-time communication or clarification between laboratories and 
payers, and rigid date-based controls that do not reflect laboratory service delivery or specimen 
handling realities. These gaps are exacerbated in rare disease and pediatric populations, where 
testing decisions are clinically time-sensitive and loss to follow up is common. 
 
There are significant opportunities for technology to mitigate these issues. Standardized, 
interoperable prior authorization platforms could improve transparency by providing real-time 
status updates, consistent criteria presentation, and alignment between authorization and 
claims adjudication. Automated and AI-enabled tools could support more efficient review by 
analyzing submitted medical records against payer criteria, identifying incomplete or 
inconsistent information prior to submission, and flagging unusual ordering or utilization 
patterns that may warrant additional scrutiny. Such approaches would allow payers to focus 
manual review on outlier or high-risk cases while reducing administrative burden and delays for 
routine, medically appropriate testing. When designed thoughtfully, technology can strengthen 
program integrity, improve access, and better align prior authorization processes with the 
clinical and operational realities of laboratory services. 
 
â— How do the issues associated with prior authorization impact the health care workforce 
and retention of skilled health care professionals 
The American Medical Association reports that 89% of physicians say that Prior Authorization 
contribute to burnout.  Physicians deal with an average of 39 prior authorizations per week and 
hire significant staff just to support prior authorizations1. The additional administrative time 
required to complete prior authorizations overburdens a workforce already struggling to meet 
clinical care needs of their patients. The additional administrative staff required to address 
these tasks adds operational costs to the clinic. Altogether, this reduces job satisfaction and 
retention of the workforce.

analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** GeneDx, LLC
- **Stakeholder type:** Technology Vendor
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Laboratory/genomic testing company with experience submitting prior authorizations for genomic tests and working with payer billing/coding requirements.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

GeneDx responds primarily to CMS's RFI on laboratory tests and DMEPOS prior authorization. It argues that current lab PA rules, especially pre-collection authorization and specimen collection date-of-service policies, misalign with genomic testing workflows, burden providers and patients, delay diagnoses, and restrict access for rare disease and pediatric populations; GeneDx recommends allowing laboratories to initiate PA, accepting test requisition forms as medical documentation where sufficiently detailed, automating documentation and payer communications, and aligning PA systems with claims and laboratory workflows.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** GENERAL/RFI; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY by analogy; API-USAGE-METRICS indirectly.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** None.
- **Standards referenced:** Electronic prior authorization in pharmacy benefit space by analogy; no specific FHIR IGs or NCPDP standards named.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Lab PA burden and date-of-service rules**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Requiring ordering providers to obtain PA before specimen collection forces additional visits, delays testing, and may prevent testing entirely.
- **Specific request:** Do not treat specimen collection date as the operative service date for PA timing; allow workflows where samples are collected and held while authorization is pursued.

**Topic 2: Laboratory-initiated PA**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Laboratories understand payer-specific coding and billing requirements and bear financial risk if authorization is denied.
- **Specific request:** Permit laboratories to initiate PA on behalf of ordering providers and patients using supplied clinical documentation.

**Topic 3: Test requisition forms as documentation**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support/Modify
- **Rationale:** TRFs can capture medical necessity information and reduce medical-record submission burden.
- **Specific request:** Allow sufficiently detailed provider-completed TRFs as medical documentation, with safeguards against fraud and support from clinical records when requested.

**Topic 4: Laboratory benefit managers**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Clarify/Modify
- **Rationale:** LBMs can consolidate payer criteria but also create hidden payer-specific deviations, appeal confusion, and feedback loops.
- **Specific request:** Improve transparency and communication among payers, LBMs, laboratories, and providers regarding criteria, billing requirements, appeals, and claim edits.

**Topic 5: Automation and AI-enabled PA**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support/Modify
- **Rationale:** Automation can reduce turnaround time, incomplete submissions, and inconsistent review while preserving program integrity.
- **Specific request:** Automate intake, documentation validation, missing-information flags, payer communication, medical-record review against criteria, and fraud/waste/abuse pattern detection.

**Topic 6: Technology gaps**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** PA systems often do not align with claims logic, clinical workflows, status visibility, or real-time communication needs.
- **Specific request:** Develop standardized interoperable PA platforms with real-time status, consistent criteria, and alignment between authorization and claims adjudication.

**Topic 7: Workforce impact**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** PA workload contributes to burnout, staffing costs, and retention problems.
- **Specific request:** Reduce PA administrative burden through automation and process reform.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S66-S82:** GeneDx directly responds to CMS's RFI on laboratory tests and DMEPOS prior authorization, including impacts on care and burden, TRFs, specimen collection timing, LBMs, automation, technology gaps, and workforce effects.
- **S29/S30:** By analogy, the comment supports metrics and technology capable of detecting incomplete submissions, status, utilization trends, and fraud/waste/abuse, but does not address drug API usage metrics directly.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Permit laboratories to initiate PA for lab testing using provider-supplied clinical documentation.
2. Stop requiring PA submission before specimen collection for genomic testing workflows.
3. Recognize that laboratory testing proceeds when analysis begins, not necessarily on collection date.
4. Allow sufficiently detailed provider-completed TRFs to demonstrate medical necessity.
5. Add safeguards to prevent fraudulent TRF use without penalizing established laboratories.
6. Improve transparency into LBM and payer criteria, claim edits, billing requirements, and appeals pathways.
7. Automate PA intake, documentation validation, status communication, and missing-information detection.
8. Use AI-enabled tools to compare medical records to payer criteria and detect unusual utilization patterns.
9. Align authorization systems, claims logic, clinical workflows, and laboratory specimen realities.
10. Reduce PA burden to improve workforce satisfaction and retention.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Provider-only PA workflows, pre-collection PA rules, arbitrary specimen date-of-service policies, LBM opacity, lack of status visibility, and payer/claims misalignment.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Delayed diagnosis, missed testing, loss to follow-up, delayed treatment, access restrictions for rare disease families, patient travel burden, and workforce burnout.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Payer-specific CPT coding schemes, specimen handling requirements, physician office inability to store specimens, LBM customization, unclear appeals pathways, and inconsistent criteria.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** GeneDx internal data shows a relatively significant number of PAs denied due to submission after collection date; AMA reports 89% of physicians say PA contributes to burnout and physicians handle an average of 39 PAs per week.
- **Studies or research referenced:** AMA prior authorization burden resource.
- **Examples provided:** Germline genomic testing, blood or buccal samples, NICU and prenatal genomic testing, rare disease patients, specimen stabilization/DNA extraction, payer recommendations to retain specimens in physician offices.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Patients needing genomic testing, rare disease families, pediatric/NICU/prenatal patients, ordering providers, laboratories, payers, LBMs, and physician office staff.
- **Economic implications:** Laboratories bear non-payment risk when authorization is denied; provider offices face staffing costs; automation may reduce payer and provider administrative costs.
- **Technical feasibility:** GeneDx sees automation and AI-enabled review as feasible when focused on documentation and administrative components rather than simplistic diagnosis/procedure codes.
- **Patient care impact:** Significant; delayed or missed genomic testing can delay diagnosis, treatment, and family answers.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Concerned and solution-oriented
- **Tone:** Technical, operational, professional
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Sample collection date is an arbitrary date of service for genomic testing." - Context: Criticizing pre-collection PA requirements.
2. "Treating specimen collection as an irreversible 'date of service' misaligns utilization management policy with clinical reality." - Context: Explaining access barriers.
3. "Automation of the prior authorization process for laboratory tests and DMEPOS items has significant potential to improve patient outcomes." - Context: Supporting automated PA.
4. "Technology has also not adequately addressed inconsistencies across payers and laboratory benefit managers." - Context: Identifying unresolved system gaps.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Discusses laboratory non-payment risk, provider staffing costs, and operational burden.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Ordering providers face PA workflow, coding, documentation, and specimen management burdens.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Rare disease and complex-condition patients face disproportionate travel and access barriers.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Proposes automation and AI-enabled PA workflows for laboratory services.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Delayed or missed testing affects diagnosis and treatment.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Highlights payer, LBM, laboratory, and provider coordination failures.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Calls for clear criteria, status visibility, and claims/authorization alignment.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Focuses on specimen collection, laboratory operations, and current PA submission pathways.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Laboratory vendors and LBMs are central stakeholders.
